units.t: The Oceans. Episode three.
In this episode: Whales: giants of the sea, The alien intelligence of octopuses and The Great Barrier Reef.
Part one. Whales: giants of the sea.
The largest animal that has ever lived swims in our oceans, and humpbacks pass Australia's coast every winter singing songs that change each year.
Mammals that went back.
Whales breathe air, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and feed them milk.
They evolved from four-legged land mammals roughly 50 million years ago, and fossils such as Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal from what is now Pakistan, show early stages.
Their front limbs became flippers, their back legs shrank to tiny internal bones and their nostrils moved to the top of the head as blowholes.
DNA studies show their closest living relatives are hippopotamuses.
Whales, dolphins and porpoises together are called cetaceans, in two groups.
Baleen whales, such as blue, humpback and southern right whales, have hundreds of keratin plates, like your fingernails, in the upper jaw to strain krill from water, and two blowholes.
Toothed whales, including sperm whales, orcas and dolphins, have one blowhole, hunt individual prey and mostly use echolocation.
Record breakers.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, larger than any dinosaur found so far.
It can reach around 30 metres and well over 100 tonnes, and its heart alone can weigh around 180 kilograms.
Pygmy blue whales feed in Australian waters, including off Perth and in the Bonney Upwelling off South Australia and Victoria.
The sperm whale has the largest brain of any animal and dives to depths of over a kilometre to hunt squid.
Some bowhead whales in the Arctic are thought to live for more than 200 years.
The humpback highway.
Humpback whales travel each year between feeding grounds in Antarctic waters and breeding grounds in the tropics, one of the longest mammal migrations.
One Australian population travels up the east coast to waters inside and near the Great Barrier Reef; the other heads up the west coast to the Kimberley.
The northern migration runs roughly May to August, and the return south, often with calves, from about August to November.
Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs, mostly on the breeding grounds.
All males in a population sing roughly the same song, which slowly changes.
Researchers found new songs can sweep east across the South Pacific, from eastern Australia to French Polynesia, within a year or two, a kind of cultural transmission rare outside humans.
Whaling and recovery.
Whaling was one of colonial Australia's earliest export industries, from the early 1800s.
By the early 1960s the east coast population had collapsed to perhaps a few hundred animals, and the east coast stations closed in 1962.
Australia's last whaling station, at Cheynes Beach near Albany in WA, closed in 1978.
The International Whaling Commission agreed a moratorium on commercial whaling in 1982, effective from 1986.
Protected from hunting, the east coast humpbacks now number in the tens of thousands, and in 2022 they were removed from the national threatened list.
Other species, such as blue whales, remain far below their pre-whaling numbers.
Watching whales well.
Australia is one of the best places in the world to watch whales, from shore, boats or planes.
To protect them, there are legal approach distances.
Vessels must generally stay at least 100 metres away, with larger distances for mothers with calves in many states, and swimmers, jet skis and drones have their own limits.
Rules vary slightly by state, so check before heading out.
If you see a stranded, injured or entangled whale, do not try to free it yourself.
Call your state's wildlife or marine rescue hotline, as entangled whales can be extremely dangerous.
The key idea: Whales are mammals that evolved from land animals about 50 million years ago, and their closest living relatives are hippos.
Part two. The alien intelligence of octopuses.
An animal that thinks with its arms, tastes with its suckers, changes colour while colour-blind and escapes from aquariums.
An alien intelligence.
Octopuses are molluscs, related to snails and clams.
Our last common ancestor with them was probably a small worm-like creature that lived over 500 million years ago.
That means octopus intelligence evolved completely independently of ours.
Philosopher Peter Godfrey-Smith, who spent years diving with octopuses off the New South Wales coast, describes them as the closest thing we'll meet to an intelligent alien.
Studying them helps scientists understand what minds are, and the different ways they can be built.
Thinking arms, tasting skin.
An octopus has around 500 million neurons, similar to a dog.
But about two thirds are in its eight arms, not its central brain.
Each arm has its own cluster of neurons that can process information and control movement semi-independently.
An arm can explore a crevice and decide to grab something while the central brain focuses elsewhere.
Even a severed arm can react to touch and grasp food for a while.
A common octopus has up to around 2,000 suckers, each packed with chemical receptors, so octopuses 'taste' what they touch.
In 2020, researchers described receptors that let them detect chemicals on surfaces and identify prey hidden in cracks without seeing it.
A very different body.
Octopuses have three hearts.
Two pump blood through the gills; the third pumps it around the rest of the body.
That third heart stops when the octopus swims, which is partly why they tire quickly and prefer crawling.
Their blood uses a copper-based protein called haemocyanin to carry oxygen, which makes it blue, and it works well in cold, low-oxygen water.
They also have no bones.
Their only hard part is a parrot-like beak, so they can squeeze through any gap larger than it.
In 2016, an octopus named Inky escaped from New Zealand's National Aquarium through a gap in his tank, crossed the floor and slid down a drainpipe into the sea.
Masters of disguise.
Octopuses can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in a fraction of a second.
Thousands of pigment cells called chromatophores, each controlled by tiny muscles and nerves, expand or shrink to show colour.
Other cells reflect light to create shimmering or white effects, and muscles raise bumps and spikes to mimic rocks or seaweed.
Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, having only one type of light receptor.
Scientists are still working out how they match colours so well.
Clever but short-lived.
Octopuses can learn to unscrew jar lids, even from the inside, navigate mazes and recognise individual humans, sometimes squirting water at people they dislike.
In Indonesia, veined octopuses have been filmed carrying coconut shell halves and assembling them into portable shelters, a rare example of tool use by an invertebrate.
Off New South Wales, gloomy octopuses live in small communities nicknamed Octopolis and Octlantis.
Yet most octopuses live only one to two years, and many species breed once and then die.
One deep-sea octopus was seen brooding her eggs for four and a half years, the longest known of any animal.
Why evolve a big, costly brain for so short a life?
It remains a mystery.
The key idea: Octopuses evolved intelligence separately from vertebrates, so studying them shows the different ways a mind can be built.
Part three. The Great Barrier Reef.
The largest structure built by living things on Earth is made by animals smaller than your fingernail, and it is under more pressure than ever.
Animals and algae.
Coral may look like rock or plants, but it is made of animals.
Each coral is a colony of thousands of tiny polyps, related to jellyfish and sea anemones.
Each polyp has stinging tentacles for catching plankton at night and builds a hard cup of limestone beneath itself.
Over generations, colonies grow on the skeletons of those before them, creating reefs large enough to be seen from space.
Reef-building corals have a secret partner: microscopic algae called zooxanthellae that live in their tissues.
They photosynthesise and share sugars, supplying most of the coral's energy, often cited as up to about 90%, and much of its colour.
In return they get shelter and nutrients.
This is why reefs grow in clear, sunlit, shallow water.
Size and diversity.
The Great Barrier Reef stretches roughly 2,300 kilometres along the Queensland coast, from the Torres Strait to near Bundaberg, and its marine park covers an area larger than Italy.
It is around 3,000 individual reefs and hundreds of islands and cays.
It supports over 400 kinds of hard coral, more than 1,500 species of fish, six of the world's seven marine turtle species, dugongs, sharks and thousands of molluscs.
Every spring, a few nights after a full moon, many corals spawn at once.
Reefs have grown along this coast for hundreds of thousands of years.
The living reef began forming around 8,000 years ago, as rising seas flooded the shelf after the last ice age.
More than 70 Traditional Owner groups hold ongoing connections to its sea country.
Coral bleaching.
When sea temperatures stay just one or two degrees above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the coral-algae partnership breaks down.
The coral expels its algae and turns white, revealing its skeleton through clear tissue.
This is bleaching.
Bleached corals are not dead, and if temperatures fall soon enough they can regain their algae and recover.
If heat stress is severe or prolonged, they starve and die.
The reef had mass bleaching in 1998 and 2002, then in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, with 2016 and 2017 killing a large share of shallow-water corals.
The main threats.

Scientists and the reef's managers agree climate change is the greatest threat, through marine heatwaves that cause bleaching and ocean acidification, which makes it harder for corals to build skeletons.
Other pressures add up.
Runoff from farms and land clearing carries sediment and fertiliser that cloud the water and can fuel outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish, which eat coral.
Stronger cyclones smash reefs apart.
Recovery takes years, often a decade or more for slow-growing corals, and the gaps between events have been getting shorter.
Parts of the reef have recovered well between events, but that resilience is being tested.
Protecting the reef.
The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park was created in 1975, following public campaigns against oil drilling and mining on the reef.
In 1981 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.
In 2004 the park was rezoned so about a third became green zones where fishing and collecting are banned, one of the largest such networks in the world.
UNESCO has several times considered listing the reef as 'in danger', which Australian governments have argued against.
In 1770, James Cook's Endeavour ran aground on it near present-day Cooktown.
Visiting well helps.
Choose eco-certified operators, never touch or stand on coral, follow zoning rules and take all rubbish home.
Some sunscreen ingredients can harm coral in lab studies, though their real-world impact is debated and small next to warming.
The biggest help is cutting emissions and improving water quality.
The key idea: Corals are colonies of tiny animals that build limestone skeletons, and algae living inside them provide most of their food and colour.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do fossils and DNA show about where whales came from?
Answer. They evolved from four-legged land mammals.
Question two. Why is octopus intelligence so interesting to scientists?
Answer. It evolved separately from ours.
Question three. What are corals?
Answer. Colonies of tiny animals.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
